concerns.text: FR-004 and US3 explicitly mandate 'bootstrap resampling (≥ 100 iterations)' for robustness. The tasks (T028, T028a) implement 'Leave-One-Out (LOO) Jackknife' (N iterations) instead. While the plan.md justifies this switch, the spec.md (FR-004) has not been updated to reflect this methodological change. The tasks silently weaken the FR-004 constraint by substituting a different statistical protocol without a corresponding spec amendment, violating the requirement that tasks must not relax what the spec demands.

FR-001 mandates handling missing values via 'linear interpolation'. Task T013 implements 'spline-based imputation' with linear interpolation only as a fallback. While the plan.md notes this as an override to preserve derivative structure, the spec.md (FR-001) remains unchanged. The task delivers a solution that does not match the spec's explicit requirement, constituting a semantic weakening of FR-001.

FR-005 requires calculating stability metrics comparing subsamples to the full ensemble. Task T030 flags unstable modes based on a correlation threshold of '< 0.95' derived from 'Constitution Principle VI'. However, Constitution Principle VI (Ensemble Robustness) states results must be 'stable against subsampling' but does not define a specific numerical threshold (0.95). The task introduces a specific acceptance criterion (0.95) not found in the spec or constitution, creating a silent drift in the definition of 'robustness' that may not align with the intended scientific rigor.

US2-AC2 (in spec.md) requires reporting cumulative variance for 'top components' and stopping if '>= 80%'. Task T023 implements this logic but hardcodes the 80% threshold. The spec's 'Assumptions' section mentions a sensitivity analysis will sweep thresholds (70%, 80%, 90%). The task as written only implements the 80% path, potentially failing to deliver the full scope of the sensitivity analysis implied by the spec's assumptions, or at least not explicitly verifying the sensitivity requirement in the task description.
